context_blurb:
Twice a day on most coasts, the sea climbs the beach and then slides away again. These rises and falls are the tides, and fishermen, sailors and swimmers plan their days around them.

Many people guess that the wind drives the tides. It does not: a storm wind can pile water against a shore, but wind changes from day to day and could never keep the tides' steady timetable. Tides come mainly from the pull of the Moon's gravity. The Moon tugs on Earth's oceans and draws the water up into a broad bulge, and as Earth turns, each coast is carried into the high water and out of it again.

Strangely, there is high water on the far side of Earth at the same time. The Moon pulls hardest on the near side of Earth and most weakly on the far side. So as the whole planet is drawn toward the Moon, the water on the far side is left behind, rising into high water there too: a second bulge. The low tides lie in the low places between the bulges. Earth spins through both bulges, so most coasts get two high tides and two low tides each day.

A tide table, the timetable of the tides that sailors and fishermen carry, shows the rhythm. On most coasts the high tides come about 12 hours and 25 minutes apart, with low water about halfway between. Two such gaps add up to a day and 50 minutes, so each day's high tide comes about 50 minutes later than the day before's. The Moon moves on along its path around Earth, travelling the same way that Earth spins, so when Earth has made one full turn the Moon has crept ahead. The coast needs about 50 minutes more to turn back under the Moon.

The Sun raises tides as well, but they are only about half the size of the Moon's, though the Sun outweighs the Moon some twenty-seven million times over. The Sun loses out because it is much farther away from Earth, nearly 400 times farther than the Moon. A tide comes not from the pull itself but from how much harder a body pulls on Earth's near side than on its far side, and that difference fades with distance even faster than the pull does.

Around new moon, when the Moon passes between Earth and the Sun, and around full moon, when it sits on Earth's far side from the Sun, the Sun, Moon and Earth line up. The Sun's tide then adds to the Moon's: the bulges grow taller, and the extra water heaped into them comes from the low places between, so the tide table shows higher high tides and lower low tides. These are spring tides, and they come twice a month, all year round. Many people think the name belongs to the season of spring, but it does not; it comes from the water springing up.

About a week after each spring tide comes a quarter moon, first or third, when the Moon looks half lit and stands at a right angle to the Sun as seen from Earth. The Sun's pull then works across the Moon's and partly cancels it, so the tidal range, the gap in height between high and low water, is the smallest of the month: these are neap tides. Lay a tide table beside a calendar of the Moon's phases and you can check the pattern for yourself.
